parsed.hook: Woodruff Vineyard sits high in the Santa Cruz Mountains, where thin shale and sandstone soils force Pinot Noir to stay small-berried and tense. That site usually gives a cooler, more savory profile than coastal California Pinot: red fruit, forest floor, and a line of acidity that keeps the wine from feeling soft.
parsed.wine_summary:
Wind Gap built its name on site-first wines, and this Pinot Noir fits that brief because the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA is all about elevation, fog exposure, and steep, low-vigor terrain. The region’s ridgelines sit above much of the marine layer, so mornings can be cool and misty while afternoons turn bright and dry; that swing slows ripening and preserves acidity, which is exactly what gives mountain Pinot its nerve.

The 2013 and 2014 vintages both sit in a price band where Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot has to earn its keep against Russian River and Sonoma Coast bottles. What makes this one different is the mountain frame: less plush fruit, more dried herbs, tea leaf, and mineral cut from the rocky slopes. If you want Pinot Noir that tastes like a place with altitude and wind, not just ripe fruit, this is the point.
parsed.terroir_expression: Shale and sandstone dominate the named soils here, and both drain fast, leaving vines with little stored water after winter rain. That stress matters: low-yield vines tend to produce smaller berries with more skin-to-juice ratio, which means firmer tannin, darker spice tones, and a more compact palate shape. Add the Santa Cruz Mountains’ elevated ridgelines above the fog layer and you get Pinot with brisk acidity, red-cherry fruit, savory bay leaf, and a stony finish rather than sweet, sun-kissed richness.
parsed.vinification_summary: Wind Gap is known for handling Pinot Noir with a light hand: whole-cluster or partial whole-cluster fermentation is common in this style, which means some intact stems go into the fermenter to add perfume, lift, and a firmer tannic spine. That stem influence can read as dried rose, spice, and tea rather than raw green flavor when the fruit is ripe enough. The point is not to polish the wine into gloss; it is to keep the vineyard’s high-toned structure intact.
parsed.food_pairing:
Duck confit with crispy potatoes works because the wine’s acidity cuts the fat and its savory mountain notes match the browned duck skin.
Nashville hot chicken is a smart casual pairing: the berry fruit cools the chile heat, while the tannin keeps the fried crust from feeling greasy.
Mushroom risotto suits this Pinot because the wine’s earthy edge meets the mushrooms’ umami and the acidity resets the palate between creamy bites.
Seared salmon with lentils and salsa verde is a strong fine-dining match; the fish needs a red with freshness, and the herb sauce links directly to the wine’s savory profile.
Peking duck fits because the lacquered skin, spice, and sweet-salty depth mirror the wine’s red fruit and mountain-derived grip.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Rhys Bearwallow Vineyard Pinot Noir — similar mountain-grown structure, high acidity, and savory, site-driven profile.
Arnot-Roberts Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir — not the same geology, but comparable in restraint, brightness, and low-oak transparency.
Ceritas Hellenthal Vineyard Pinot Noir — shares a cool-climate, site-specific approach with firm acidity and a more savory than fruity finish.
parsed.style_profile: Cool-climate mountain Pinot Noir with medium body, firm acidity, fine tannin, and savory mineral drive
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink from now through the next 5 to 8 years if you want the wine’s red fruit and lifted aromatics. Store it cool and stable, ideally around 55°F, because this style depends on freshness more than sheer concentration.
parsed.value_assessment: $35–$55 is the right range for this bottle, and at that level it stacks up against Littorai Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir and Kosta Browne’s entry-level Pinot bottlings. It is worth the money if you want a site-specific, mountain-leaning Pinot with real structure; it is not worth it if you only want ripe, glossy California fruit.
parsed.market_position: On restaurant lists, this belongs in the section for diners who order by vineyard and appellation rather than by brand alone. Retail buyers and collectors who follow cool-climate California Pinot will recognize the appeal immediately, especially people who prefer transparent, savory wines over oak-driven style.
parsed.insider_take: The tradeoff is clear: this wine gives you tension and place, not cushion. People who expect Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot to taste like sweet strawberry and vanilla usually miss the point; the win is the stony, herbal, red-fruited shape that comes from altitude and thin soils. Buy it if you like Pinot with edge; skip it if you want softness first.
